flashcards.q: What is the core idea of an RLM?
flashcards.a: Treat the long prompt as data in an external environment rather than placing all of it in the model context. The model programmatically inspects, partitions, searches, and recursively calls itself on selected snippets.

flashcards.q: What problem does an RLM target?
flashcards.a: Context rot: quality can fall as context grows even when the input fits the nominal window. Externalizing context lets the model spend tokens on relevant slices instead of carrying every token through every reasoning step.

flashcards.q: How is an RLM different from ordinary RAG?
flashcards.a: RAG retrieves pre-indexed documents or chunks by similarity. An RLM gives the model a programmable environment over the prompt itself, allowing inspection, grep, partitioning, arbitrary code, and recursive subcalls without requiring a separate vector index.

flashcards.q: What does the external environment need to expose?
flashcards.a: At minimum: bounded peek/read, search or grep, slicing/partitioning, structured child-call execution, result collection, and a hard budget for recursion depth, calls, tokens, wall time, and output size.

flashcards.q: Why does recursive decomposition help long-context quality?
flashcards.a: It changes the computation from one flat attention problem into selective exploration plus aggregation. Child calls see smaller, task-specific snippets, reducing distractors and allowing parallel or hierarchical synthesis.

flashcards.q: What is the main cost tradeoff of an RLM?
flashcards.a: It spends extra model calls and orchestration overhead to reduce context dilution. Total cost can be comparable when the baseline would send huge prompts, but poorly bounded recursion can multiply calls and latency.

flashcards.q: Why must child calls return structured results?
flashcards.a: Free-form child prose is hard to aggregate and can duplicate or contradict facts. Typed outputs such as claims, counts, evidence spans, confidence, and errors let the parent combine results deterministically and detect partial failure.

flashcards.q: What is an RLM failure mode that ordinary context-window tuning hides?
flashcards.a: A child-call explosion can exceed cost or time budgets while every individual call looks healthy. Instrument recursion depth, fan-out, cumulative tokens, wall time, and cancellation propagation, not only model latency per call.

flashcards.q: How should an RLM handle untrusted context?
flashcards.a: Treat external text as data, not instructions. Restrict the environment's tools, validate child-call arguments, preserve provenance for slices, sandbox code execution, and enforce the same action-layer permissions used for agents.

flashcards.q: When is ordinary long-context prompting still preferable?
flashcards.a: When the context is modest, the task needs global stylistic or relational reasoning, and extra calls would cost more than they save. RLMs add orchestration complexity and are not a universal replacement for a large context window.

flashcards.q: What should an RLM eval compare?
flashcards.a: Compare vanilla long-context, compaction, retrieval, code-execution scaffolds, and RLM arms on the same tasks. Report answer quality, evidence recall, cost, latency, call count, failure rate, and sensitivity to context length.

flashcards.q: What does two orders of magnitude beyond the context window mean operationally?
flashcards.a: The external environment can hold inputs much larger than the model's nominal context, but the model still sees bounded slices and summaries. It does not mean the model attends to all tokens simultaneously or that quality is automatically preserved.
